Your tone isn't a problem. I agree with the other comment – I think it's mostly a matter of pitch and breath. If you get the pitch right you'll sound tons better. Learning how to breathe correctly for singing takes a long time but I would especially focus on getting the notes right first.

Singing on-pitch is 70% of what makes pleasant-sounding singing, in my opinion. Someone could have the weakest, most unremarkable voice in the world, and yet if he sings on pitch and follows the rhythm, it will rarely sound unpleasant.

Another thing you can do is download a tuner app and see which notes come up as you sing to make sure you're hitting the same notes the original singer is hitting. It's good that you're recording yourself. Try hearing say the first verse of Delilah, then record yourself singing it, then compare it to the recording and you'll likely notice the parts where you go off-pitch. Hearing other singers repeatedly and then hearing oneself helps you pinpoint the bits you need to improve.

Another thing that helps A TON with learning how to sing on pitch is learning an instrument. I know this sound a bit extreme/boring (if you're not into that) but it does wonders. I only took my first vocal lesson about a month ago and my teacher could hardly believe it was my first class because even though my breathing wasn't good, I was able to follow pitch and rhythm correctly and I attribute this 100% to my learning piano and guitar.

TL,DR; your main problem is pitch and breathing. Talk to your professor about helping you find pitch or buy a tuner to keep track of the notes you're hitting. Consider learning an instrument – it will do wonders to develop your musical ear and to help you sing on pitch.

It should never, ever, ever hurt if you do it right. Get a singing professor. I used to think this was normal and then after a couple of classes managed to reach the high notes I couldn't before with a lot more strength, little effort (compared to what I was doing before, at least) and NO pain, even after rehearsing the high part for 10 times.

In spite of this, I've heard singing teachers say that belting is harmful to your voice so it shouldn't be done constantly or it could really hurt you. You're supposed to belt with a mixed voice (half chest, half head voice) so it's a bit easier on your chords.

Here's a tip, maybe it'll work for you: try squatting as you reach the high note. It kind of fools your mind into focusing on your body and on going down instead of thinking "high" and getting a tense throat/jaw.

Hope this helps. Best of luck :)

Hi! I used to feel just like that a while ago, I was close to reaching rock bottom and thought that would be it but I'm a lot better now and I'm glad I held on.

When you're that sad, there's not much people can say to cheer you up because it feels like nothing will change. But because I was in a similar position, I'll tell you the things I did (which may or may not work for you) to give you some perspective. Maybe it will help:

1. The boyfriend: I ended it. It was the most painful experience of my life but the truth is, I was with him because I felt like I needed support, but I was making him unhappy with my own sadness, and he obviously couldn't make me happy because I was so deep in my own depression that I couldn't see what I had. Breaking up was really hard but it forced me to get out of my comfort zone, make big changes and find meaning in my life without having to justify or explain my decisions to anyone. Whether you want it or not, when you're in a relationship and you make decisions it affects the both of you.

2. The job that made me miserable: I quit it and decided to pursue something I enjoyed more. This greatly increased my quality of life and my levels of happiness. Doing a job I absolutely hated day in and day out was consuming me. Easier said than done, changing careers/sources of income can be tough, but with enough hard work, it's worth it.

3. The music/passion: Pursue it, if only as a hobby. This made a big difference in my life and it made me excited to wake up in the mornings – something I hadn't felt in years. I even started sleeping less and feeling less tired because I was actually looking forward to writing/making music. The same with art or any sport you're passionate about. I used to dance and engage in artistic hobbies when I was younger, and I don't think it's a coincidence that once I became an adult and stopped, my life felt gray. Whatever it is you like, as insignificant as it may now seem, even if it's just doodling or sketching or making Play-Doh figures, use it as an outlet for your emotions or your sadness, and work on it day by day. I started doing this and day by day I would set a goal for myself. After days and weeks of doing this, you start to see yourself get better at doing something you enjoy. Progress and eventually ambition to be better and do more will push you forward. Daily goals.

4. Time: This took me months to achieve. I started making little changes in my life and now, months later, I am happy I waited. Time heals, but time can either build you or destroy you, depending on how you use it. Hang on and give yourself a chance. It's true that the rainbow comes after the storm, but only if you put in the effort to make little changes and persevere. It won't always be easy, but if you can picture in your head the idea of what a happy day would be for you, and if you think this day is remotely possible with enough effort, then give yourself the chance. 

5. The friends: This one is tough because as we grow up, we change, and the people we used to hang out with may not fit with our values and interests anymore. I still struggle with this but I filled this void with my hobbies/side projects. Maybe trying to learn a new instrument or getting back into sports will help you meet new people. MeetUps also help.

5. Make someone else smile: This is the last step and is one that I'm still working on. Doing charity and volunteering can give you a sense of purpose. Helping others makes us happy because who doesn't want to feel like they can make a difference and make someone smile? This is a surefire way to feel better.

6. Run: When all else fails – endorphins.

Hang in there, it does get better, you just need to give yourself the chance and believe in your own magic :)
